title: Chains That Spread the Good News
sum: Paul writes from prison to the church he founded in Philippi, a Roman colony in northern Greece. He opens with thanks: from the first day the Philippians have been his partners in the good news, and he is sure God will finish the work he began in them (1:3-11). Then he reports on his own situation. His chains have not stopped the message; they have made it known among the soldiers who guard him, and other believers have grown bold (1:12-14). Some preach out of rivalry, hoping to hurt him, but Paul rejoices that Christ is announced at all (1:15-18).

Paul does not know whether his trial will end in release or death, and he weighs both: 'For me, living is Christ and dying is gain' (1:21). He would rather go and be with Christ, but he expects to stay for their sake (1:22-26). The chapter ends with the letter's main appeal: live as citizens worthy of the good news, stand firm together, do not be frightened, and see suffering for Christ as a gift (1:27-30).
readings: Read as a friendship letter

Greek writers had a form for letters between friends: shared feelings, longing to see each other, news of one's own affairs, and a common cause. Philippians 1 has all of these. Paul is not asserting authority (he does not even call himself an apostle); he speaks as a partner, and expects them to care about his news as he cares about theirs.
Read as a prisoner's testimony

The chapter can also be read as the statement of a man awaiting a verdict that might be death. His 'defense' (1:7, 17) is a court word. On this reading the chapter is about how a believer faces a hostile court and the possibility of execution: with joy, with freedom of speech, and with the conviction that Christ will be honored either way.

views.H: Philippi was refounded as a Roman colony after the battle of 42 BC, with veterans settled on its land, and it was a 'miniature Rome' full of Latin inscriptions. Paul founded the church on his second journey, likely about AD 49 or 50 (Acts 16). Now he is a prisoner. Where? Rome (about AD 62), Ephesus (about 52-55) and Caesarea (about 57-59) are all proposed. The 'praetorium' (1:13) and 'Caesar's household' (4:22) fit Rome most easily, but both terms were used in the provinces too. The answer affects the date and how many journeys between Philippi and Paul's prison the letter assumes (Epaphroditus' trip, the news of his illness, the planned visits of Timothy and Paul).
views.C: Almost all scholars agree that Paul wrote Philippians. The questions are its unity (one letter or several joined: see 3:1 and the book page) and its place of writing. Chapter 1 also raises the question of the 'overseers and deacons' (1:1): early evidence of church offices, or a later addition? The words are in every edition of the Greek used here.
views.L: The chapter follows the usual shape of a Pauline letter opening: greeting (1:1-2), thanksgiving and prayer (1:3-11), then the body. Words that will matter later appear here first: joy (1:4), partnership (1:5), think (1:7), the day of Christ (1:6, 10), live as citizens (1:27), one soul (1:27), struggle (1:30). The chapter turns at 1:27 from Paul's news to his appeal.
views.J: Paul's 'salvation' in 1:19 quotes the Greek of Job 13:16 exactly: Job, the righteous sufferer on trial, is sure of his vindication. The 'day of Christ' adapts the prophets' day of the LORD. 'I will not be put to shame' (1:20) is the language of the Psalms. Philippi had no synagogue that Acts mentions, only 'a place of prayer' by a river (Acts 16:13), and the church's first believer, Lydia, 'worshiped God' as a Gentile who joined in Jewish prayer (Acts 16:14).
views.T: John Chrysostom preached a series of homilies on Philippians, and Calvin wrote a commentary on it. Calvin reads 1:1 as showing several bishops in one church and calls 'bishop' and 'pastor' the same office; Catholic and Orthodox readers see in the same verse the roots of the later order of bishops, priests and deacons. 1:21-24 has been central for teaching on what happens at death (see the card); 1:6 for teaching on assurance and perseverance.

deep.b:
Paul says he is in chains (1:7, 13, 14, 16) and facing a verdict that could mean death (1:20-23). He does not say where. Three places are proposed.

Rome, about AD 62. The traditional view, and often judged the most likely. Acts ends with Paul under guard in Rome for two years (Acts 28:16, 30-31). 'The whole praetorium' (1:13) fits the Praetorian Guard, and 'Caesar's household' (4:22) fits the imperial staff in the capital. A church with overseers and deacons (1:1) and a prisoner who expects a final verdict, possibly death (1:20-23), suit a later date. The subscription in the Textus Receptus says 'written from Rome'.

Ephesus, about AD 52-55. Acts mentions no imprisonment there, but Paul speaks of many imprisonments (2 Corinthians 11:23) and of deadly danger in Asia (1 Corinthians 15:32). Ephesus is much nearer to Philippi, which suits the several journeys the letter assumes. The governor's headquarters could be called a praetorium, and imperial slaves served in the provinces. Michael Flexsenhar (2019) has argued that the imperial slaves Paul means were in Asia Minor.

Caesarea, about AD 57-59. Acts says Paul was 'held under guard in Herod's Praetorium' (Acts 23:35) and kept for two years (Acts 24:27). But Caesarea is far from Philippi, and there Paul could appeal to Caesar (Acts 25:11), so to some readers a final verdict of death there seems less likely.

The choice changes the date, the order of Paul's letters, and how we picture the trips of Epaphroditus and Timothy. It does not change the letter's message.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the letter's 'citizenship' frame begins in 1:27 and ends in 3:20-21
deep.b: The verb and noun of citizenship that Paul uses here, politeuomai 'live as citizens' (1:27) and politeuma 'commonwealth' (3:20), occur nowhere else in his letters (Ephesians 2:12 and 2:19 use related words, and Acts 23:1 has Paul use the verb in a speech). Between them stand the hymn (2:6-11), Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples (2:19-30), and Paul's own story (3:4-14). It may be that Paul built the middle of the letter as an answer to one question a Roman colony would ask: what does a good citizen look like? His answer is a person who, like Christ, does not use status for himself. This overlaps with Joseph Hellerman's reading of the hymn against Roman honor culture (Reconstructing Honor in Roman Philippi, 2005), but the claim that 1:27 and 3:20 frame the letter's structure is my own suggestion. The partition theories, which cut the letter at 3:1, would make the frame accidental.

echoes: Acts 16:9-40; Acts 28:16-31; Job 13:16; Job 13:18; Psalm 25:2-3; Amos 5:18; Romans 1:8-13; Romans 8:19; 2 Corinthians 5:6-9; 1 Thessalonians 1:2-3; 1 Thessalonians 2:2; 1 Thessalonians 4:13-17

settings.by: Paul and Timothy, as the letter names them
settings.to: the church at Philippi, a Roman colony in Macedonia: mostly Gentile believers, men and women, meeting in homes such as Lydia's (Acts 16:15, 40), with overseers and deacons
settings.when: while Paul is a prisoner awaiting a verdict, some years after he founded the church in about AD 49 or 50: about twelve years if he wrote from Rome (about AD 62, the traditional view), two to six from Ephesus (AD 52-55), seven to ten from Caesarea (AD 57-59)
settings.why: to greet the whole church, with its leaders, as 'saints' and partners. Paul does not use the title 'apostle' here: he writes as a friend and fellow slave of Christ, not to assert authority. Naming the overseers and deacons may thank the leaders who organized the gift Epaphroditus brought (4:10-18).
views: Written from Rome during the custody described in Acts 28, about AD 62; the praetorium is the Praetorian Guard and 'Caesar's household' the imperial staff; a developed church with overseers and deacons and a prisoner facing a possible death sentence suit a later date.
Written from an imprisonment in Ephesus, about AD 52-55, not told in Acts; nearer to Philippi, which suits the trips the letter assumes.
Written from Herod's Praetorium in Caesarea, about AD 57-59 (Acts 23:35; 24:27).

settings.when: at the start of the letter, after the church's gift has reached him
settings.why: to tell the church how he thanks God for their partnership from the first day, how sure he is that God will finish what he began, and what he prays for them: love that grows with insight, so they can tell what matters most. The prayer sets out the themes of the letter, joy, partnership, thinking rightly, and the day of Christ. For a church facing opposition and quarrels, it is both comfort and gentle direction.

settings.when: as he waits for his trial, uncertain whether it will end in release or death
settings.why: to answer their worry. They had sent help and wanted news. Paul tells them that his chains have spread the good news, that he rejoices even over rival preachers, and that he is ready either to live or to die. The report is also a model for them: in 1:30 he says their struggle is the same as his. Knowing that the first readers had seen him beaten and jailed in their own city (Acts 16:22-24) makes the report personal, not abstract.

settings.what: The appeal to live as citizens worthy of the good news
settings.to: the whole church at Philippi, under pressure from opponents in the city
settings.when: at the turn from Paul's news to his instructions
settings.why: to state the main appeal of the letter: unity and courage. In a Roman colony where citizenship was a prized status, Paul tells them to 'live as citizens' of the good news. The opponents are probably outsiders, townspeople and authorities hostile to a new cult, as in Acts 16:19-24. Paul calls the church's suffering a gift and a sign of salvation, so they will not read it as a sign that God has left them.

traditions.q: Philippi has 'overseers and deacons' (1:1), several overseers in one church. Does this show the order of bishop, priest and deacon, or one office of elder-overseer?
views: The ministry instituted by God is exercised in degrees 'called bishops, priests, and deacons'; bishops and priests share Christ's priesthood, and deacons serve them, and all three are conferred by ordination (Catechism 1554, which quotes Ignatius: 'Let everyone revere the deacons as Jesus Christ, the bishop as the image of the Father').

The Confession of Dositheus (1672) teaches that 'the dignity of the Bishop is so necessary in the Church' that without him there could be no Church; 'the Priest is ordained by the Bishop, but a Bishop is not ordained by a Priest', and 'the Bishop is the first minister' (decree 10).

The Church of England keeps the three orders: Article 36 of the Thirty-Nine Articles approves 'The Book of Consecration of Archbishops and Bishops, and Ordering of Priests and Deacons' and declares those so ordained 'rightly, orderly, and lawfully consecrated and ordered'.

The Treatise on the Power and Primacy of the Pope (1537) follows Jerome: 'with the exception of ordination, what does the bishop have that the elder does not?' The grades of bishop and pastor 'are not different by divine authority', so 'ordination administered by a pastor in his own church is valid' (paragraphs 62-65).

Calvin read 1:1 as showing that 'bishop' was a name common to all ministers of the word, since Paul gives 'several bishops to one Church'; the later custom of one bishop over the presbyters 'rests on no Scripture authority'. He took the deacons to be stewards of the alms.
The Southern Baptist Convention's Baptist Faith and Message (2000) names two scriptural offices, 'pastor/elder/overseer and deacon', and limits the office of pastor to men (Article VI).

traditions.q: When Paul longs 'to leave and be with Christ' (1:23), does he mean believers are with Christ, conscious, right after death? What else happens then?
views: Yes. 'Those who die in God's grace and friendship and are perfectly purified live for ever with Christ' (Catechism 1023), and 'to live in heaven is "to be with Christ"' (1025). Those who die in God's grace but 'still imperfectly purified' are 'assured of their eternal salvation' and first undergo purification, the teaching called purgatory (1030).

The Confession of Dositheus teaches that 'the souls of those that have fallen asleep are either at rest or in torment' according to their deeds, at once after death, though neither state is complete until the resurrection; some who repented but need cleansing can be helped by the prayers and the Eucharist of the church (decree 18).

At death the souls of believers, 'which neither die nor sleep', return to God; 'the souls of the righteous, being then made perfect in holiness, are received into the highest heavens', waiting for the redemption of their bodies. The Westminster Confession lists Philippians 1:23 as a proof text (32.1).

No. Seventh-day Adventists teach that the dead sleep until the resurrection: 'Until that day death is an unconscious state for all people.' On this view the next thing the believer knows after death is Christ's coming.

title: The Mind of Christ
sum: Paul turns his appeal for unity into a portrait of Christ. If their life in Christ means anything, they should think the same way, put others first, and look out for each other's interests (2:1-4). Then comes one of the most famous passages in the New Testament (2:6-11), often called the Christ hymn: being in the form of God, Christ did not count equality with God as something to exploit; he emptied himself, took a slave's form, became human, and was obedient all the way to death on a cross. Therefore God raised him to the heights and gave him the name above every name, so that every knee should bend and every tongue confess 'Jesus Christ is Lord'.

Paul draws the practical lesson: work out your salvation with fear and trembling, because God is at work in you; do not grumble like Israel in the desert; shine like lights in a twisted generation (2:12-18). Then he introduces two men who live this way: Timothy, whom he hopes to send, and Epaphroditus, the church's messenger, who nearly died serving Paul and is now coming home (2:19-30).
readings: Read as an ethical example

Most readers through history have taken the hymn as the supreme example: as Christ gave up his rights, so should we. The setting supports this: 2:3-4 asks for humility, and 2:5 says 'think this way'. Timothy and Epaphroditus (2:19-30) and Paul himself (3:4-14) follow the same pattern.
Read as the story of salvation

Others hold that the hymn is not mainly an example but the story of what God has done in Christ, which places the church under a new Lord. The church is not asked to repeat the incarnation; it is asked to live as people whose Lord is the crucified and exalted Jesus. The two readings are often combined.
Read as a Christian reading of Isaiah

Many readers hear the servant of Isaiah 52:13-53:12 behind the hymn (emptied, slave, humbled, death, raised and exalted) and Isaiah 45:23 in its climax. On this reading the hymn is early Christian interpretation of Israel's Scriptures, applied to Jesus.

views.H: In Roman Philippi honor was public and ranked: offices, titles and seats were won in a sequence and announced on inscriptions. The hymn moves the other way, from equality with God to a slave's form and a slave's death on a cross, the Roman punishment for slaves and rebels. Joseph Hellerman (Reconstructing Honor in Roman Philippi, 2005) reads the hymn as a deliberate reversal of that ladder of honor. Timothy and Epaphroditus are examples of people who, in that culture, gave up status for others.
views.C: Ernst Lohmeyer (1928) first set out 2:6-11 as a poem in stanzas, probably older than Paul, and this view has dominated study since; some think 'yes, death on a cross' (2:8) is Paul's addition. Others hold that Paul wrote it himself, and some object to calling it a 'hymn' since it has no Greek meter. Critics also debate the key words: morphe, harpagmos and ekenosen (see the notes), and whether the hymn speaks of a pre-existent Christ or contrasts Jesus with Adam (James Dunn and Oscar Cullmann stress the Adam parallel).
views.L: The hymn has two movements: Christ's own action downward (he did not exploit, he emptied himself, he made himself low) and God's action upward (God raised him, gave him the name). The center is the cross. Word links bind it to the letter: 'form' returns in 3:10 and 3:21, 'count' in 2:3 and 3:7-8, 'made himself low' in 2:3 and 3:21, 'obedient' in 2:12. Paul frames it with 'think this way' (2:5) and 'so' (2:12).
views.J: The hymn's climax takes Isaiah 45:23, where the LORD swears that every knee will bend to him, and applies it to Jesus, while ending 'for the glory of God the Father'. Many scholars see here the earliest Christians placing Jesus within the worship of Israel's one God rather than beside it. The grumbling and the 'warped and twisted generation' of 2:14-15 come from Israel's wilderness story and the Song of Moses (Deuteronomy 32:5), and the drink offering (2:17) from Israel's worship.
views.T: The hymn was central in the fourth-century debates over the Son's divinity: Chrysostom used it against the Arians, Paul of Samosata and the Marcionites. The Council of Chalcedon (451) confessed Christ in two natures 'unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably'. The Lutheran Formula of Concord and Calvin read 'emptied himself' as the concealing or non-use of the divine majesty, not its loss. In the nineteenth century Gottfried Thomasius in Germany and later Charles Gore and others in Britain proposed 'kenotic' Christologies, in which the Son limited some divine attributes; Pius XII's encyclical Sempiternus Rex Christus (1951) condemned the kenotic doctrine as 'a wicked invention' (paragraph 29). Wesley preached on 2:12-13 (Sermon 85).

deep.h: The Christ hymn, line by line
deep.b:
2:6 'Being in the form of God'. Morphe is the form in which something shows what it is. Most readers take it to mean that Christ shared God's being or glory before he became human; a minority hear an Adam contrast (Adam, made in God's image, grasped at being like God, Genesis 3:5).

'he did not count equality with God as something to exploit'. Harpagmos is rare. The KJV's 'robbery' takes it as an act of seizing; others as a prize to be seized or held. Roy Hoover (1971) argued that the idiom means 'something to take advantage of', and many recent interpreters follow him; the Plain English Translation does.

2:7 'he emptied himself'. Paul says how: by taking a slave's form and coming to be human. He does not say what was given up. That question became the debate over kenosis.

2:8 'he made himself low ... death on a cross'. Obedience to God to the lowest death the Roman world knew.

2:9-11 'That is why God also raised him to the heights'. God acts, gives the name above every name, and the whole creation bows before Jesus with the words Isaiah 45:23 reserved for the LORD. The last words, 'for the glory of God the Father', keep the confession within the worship of the one God.

deep.h: What did Christ empty himself of? The kenosis debate
deep.b:
Chrysostom answered that he emptied himself by adding, not subtracting: he took on a slave's form without ceasing to be what he was: 'If the form of God is perfect God, then the form of a servant is a perfect servant.' The Council of Chalcedon (451) set the boundaries later churches kept: one Christ in two natures, 'unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably'.

The Reformation churches asked about the divine majesty during Christ's earthly life. The Formula of Concord (Lutheran) says Christ had the majesty from his conception but, as Philippians 2:7 testifies, 'kept it concealed in the state of His humiliation and did not always use it, but only when He wanted to use it' (Solid Declaration VIII 26). Calvin: 'Christ, indeed, could not divest himself of Godhead; but he kept it concealed for a time.'

In the nineteenth century Gottfried Thomasius, the first to set out a 'kenotic Christology' by that name, and later Charles Gore, P. T. Forsyth and H. R. Mackintosh, proposed that the Son really limited some divine attributes so as to live a truly human life. Supporters say this takes Jesus' growth and limits seriously (Mark 13:32). Critics say it makes the Son cease to be fully God. Pius XII condemned the kenotic doctrine in 1951, calling the idea that 'the divinity was taken away from the Word in Christ' 'a wicked invention' (Sempiternus Rex Christus 29). The verse itself says only that he emptied himself by taking a slave's form.

echoes: Genesis 3:5; Isaiah 45:21-23; Isaiah 52:13-53:12; Isaiah 49:4; Deuteronomy 32:5; Exodus 16:7; Numbers 14:27; Numbers 15:5-10; Daniel 12:3; Matthew 23:12; Mark 10:45; John 1:1-14; John 13:4-5; Romans 5:19; Romans 14:11; 1 Corinthians 8:6; 2 Corinthians 8:9; Colossians 1:15-20; Hebrews 1:3-4; 2 Timothy 4:6

settings.what: The appeal for unity and humility
settings.to: the church at Philippi (see 1:1-2), including leaders who disagree (4:2-3)
settings.when: after the call to stand together against opponents (1:27-30)
settings.why: to tell a church under outside pressure that its first danger is inside: rivalry and conceit. Paul uses the words of 1:16 ('push yourselves forward') to set them against the rival preachers, and asks them to rank others above themselves. In a colony where people competed for honor, this was a different way to live together.

settings.by: Paul, perhaps quoting an earlier Christian hymn or creed (debated)
settings.when: as the ground of the appeal for humility
settings.why: to show the church the way of thinking that belongs to people in Christ: the one who had the highest status used it for others, took the lowest place, and was raised by God. Whether the hymn already existed or Paul wrote it, he uses it to shape how the Philippians treat each other, and to remind citizens of a Roman colony who their true Lord is.
views: Paul quotes a hymn or creed the churches already knew, perhaps sung in worship (Lohmeyer and many since; the Catechism of the Catholic Church calls it 'a hymn cited by St. Paul', 461).
Paul wrote the passage for this letter in elevated prose; the lack of meter and the close links with the rest of the letter point that way.

settings.what: Work out your salvation; lights in the world
settings.when: while Paul is absent and may die (2:17)
settings.why: to apply the hymn: as Christ obeyed, they should keep obeying, not because Paul watches but because God works in them. The echoes of Israel in the wilderness tell a Gentile church that it is part of the story of God's people on the way, and must not grumble as Israel did. Paul's picture of himself as a drink offering prepares them for his possible death.

settings.when: as Epaphroditus, recovered from a near-fatal illness, is about to return to Philippi, probably carrying this letter
settings.why: to announce visits, and to present two living examples of the hymn's way of thinking. Timothy cares for their interests, not his own; Epaphroditus risked his life for Christ's work. Paul's warm words also protect Epaphroditus from any suspicion that he failed in his task by coming home early.

traditions.q: When Christ 'emptied himself' (2:7), what did he lay aside?
views: The Catechism reads 2:5-8 as 'a hymn cited by St. Paul' about the Incarnation: the Son of God 'assumed a human nature' to accomplish our salvation (Catechism 461). Pius XII's encyclical Sempiternus Rex Christus (8 September 1951) condemned as 'a wicked invention' the kenotic idea that 'the divinity was taken away from the Word in Christ', built on 'a rashly and falsely understood sentence' of Philippians 2:7 (paragraph 29).

The Council of Chalcedon, received by the Eastern Orthodox Church, confessed one Christ 'in Two Natures unconfusedly, unchangeably, indivisibly, inseparably'; nothing of the divine nature was lost. Chrysostom, a father of the Eastern church, read the passage so: 'If the form of God is perfect God, then the form of a servant is a perfect servant.' (The Oriental Orthodox churches, Coptic, Armenian, Syriac, Ethiopian, Eritrean and Malankara, do not accept the Chalcedonian Definition; they confess Christ's divine and human natures 'united in one incarnate nature'.)

Christ had the divine majesty 'immediately at His conception', but, 'as the apostle testifies [Philippians 2:7], He laid it aside': 'He kept it concealed in the state of His humiliation and did not always use it, but only when He wanted to use it' (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VIII 26).

Calvin: the form of God 'means here his majesty'; 'Christ, indeed, could not divest himself of Godhead; but he kept it concealed for a time', so 'he laid aside his glory in the view of men, not by lessening it, but by concealing it'.

The Thirty-Nine Articles follow the creeds: the Son 'took Man's nature', 'so that two whole and perfect Natures, that is to say, the Godhead and Manhood, were joined together in one Person, never to be divided' (Article 2). Charles Gore, an Anglican bishop, was among the theologians who later proposed a kenotic Christology.

traditions.q: 'Work out your own salvation ... for the one at work in you is God' (2:12-13). How do God's work and human effort relate?
views: Grace comes first, and the person cooperates with it: 'neither is man himself utterly without doing anything' when he receives grace (Trent, session 6, chapter 5). Trent quotes this verse when it warns believers to 'work out their salvation' with fear and trembling (chapter 13), and it rejects the view that the will is merely passive (canon 4).

The Confession of Dositheus (1672) teaches that grace 'co-operates with us', and that a person 'has it in his own power to will, or not to will, to co-operate with grace', though he cannot of himself do any work worthy of a Christian life (decrees 3 and 14).

It is God who 'worketh in us both to will and to do' (Phil. 2:13, cited in the Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration II). After conversion, 'we can and should cooperate' through the Spirit's power, 'although still in great weakness', not like two horses pulling a wagon together (II 65-66).

Believers' 'ability to do good works is not at all of themselves, but wholly from the Spirit of Christ', who works in them 'to will, and to do'; yet they must stir up that grace and not grow negligent (Westminster Confession 16.3, citing 2:12-13).
Wesley preached on these verses: 'God worketh in you; therefore you can work', and 'God worketh in you; therefore you must work' (Sermon 85, 'On Working Out Our Own Salvation').

title: Everything as Loss
sum: The tone changes sharply. After 'rejoice in the Lord' Paul warns: look out for the dogs, the bad workers, the mutilation (3:1-2). Most readers take these to be teachers who wanted Gentile believers to be circumcised, though Paul never names them. Paul answers by setting out his own Jewish credentials: circumcised on the eighth day, from Israel and the tribe of Benjamin, a Pharisee, zealous, blameless in the righteousness the law speaks of (3:4-6). All this he now counts as loss, even as dung, compared with knowing Christ and having a righteousness that comes from God through faith (3:7-11).

But he has not arrived. Like a runner he puts the past out of mind and reaches for the finish line and the prize (3:12-14). He asks the church to copy him and others who live this way, and he weeps over those who walk as 'enemies of Christ's cross' (3:17-19). Against them he sets the church's true identity: 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven', from which the Lord Jesus Christ will come to transform our lowly bodies into the form of his glorious body (3:20-21).
readings: Read as Paul's life in the pattern of the hymn

Many readers see chapter 3 as Paul's own version of 2:6-11. As Christ did not exploit his status, Paul counts his status as loss; as Christ was obedient to death, Paul wants to take on 'the form of his death'; as God exalted Christ, so Christ will transform believers' bodies to 'share the form of his body of glory'. The same words (count, form, low, Lord) bind the two passages.
Read as a separate warning letter

Scholars who divide the letter see 3:2-4:1 (or 3:2-21) as part of a different, sharper letter written when teachers demanding circumcision came near Philippi. The break at 3:1-2 is their main evidence.
Read as a key text on justification

For the churches of the Reformation, 3:9 is one of the clearest statements that a person is right with God by a righteousness that comes from God through faith, not by his own. For the New Perspective, it is Paul's renunciation of the righteousness that marked him as a faithful Jew, in favor of membership in Christ open to Gentiles.

views.H: Paul's record (3:5-6) is that of a Jew of the dispersion who kept the ancestral language and the Law strictly. Philippi had few Jews: Acts mentions only a 'place of prayer' outside the gate (Acts 16:13). So the 'dogs' may have been traveling Jewish-Christian teachers like those in Galatia, rather than local people. 'A commonwealth in heaven' and 'Savior' and 'Lord' (3:20) spoke to citizens of a Roman colony whose rights came from Rome and whose emperor was hailed with such titles.
views.C: The break at 3:1-2 is the main evidence for the theory that Philippians joins two or three letters (one common proposal: 3:2-4:1 as a separate letter). The opponents are debated: Jewish-Christian missionaries demanding circumcision (the usual view), Jewish people of the city, Christian libertines (3:19), or a mix of groups. Whether 3:12 answers people who claimed to be 'perfect' already is also debated.
views.L: The chapter is built on reversals: gain and loss, past and future, earth and heaven, the body of our low state and the body of his glory. Running words (chase, catch hold, the mark, the prize) shape 3:12-14. The 'form' words (3:10, 21) and 'low state' (3:21) recall the hymn.
views.J: This chapter is easily misread against Judaism. Paul does not say his Jewish heritage was evil; he says it was 'profits' that he now counts as loss compared with Christ. He still names himself a Hebrew and of the tribe of Benjamin, as in Romans 11:1. 'The dogs' (3:2) has been used as a slur against Jews: John Chrysostom called the dogs Jews and said the name, once given to Gentiles, now belonged to the Jews (Homily 10). The most common modern reading is that Paul means Jewish-Christian teachers who would require circumcision of Gentile believers; some think of local Jews or of other groups (see the deep dive). Paul's own pride in his descent (3:5) tells against using the verse against the Jewish people. The New Perspective reads 'my own righteousness' as covenant status, not self-earned merit.
views.T: 3:9 is a central text for the Reformation doctrine of a righteousness from God counted to the believer (Augsburg Confession IV), and for the Catholic teaching that God's righteousness makes the believer truly righteous (Trent, session 6, chapter 7). 3:12-15 is the text of Wesley's sermon 'Christian Perfection'. 3:20-21 has been central for teaching on the bodily resurrection.

deep.h: Who were the opponents of chapter 3?
deep.b:
Paul does not name them, so readers have reconstructed them from his words.

Teachers demanding circumcision. The most common view. 'The mutilation' (3:2) is a mocking pun on circumcision, and Paul answers with his own Jewish credentials (3:4-6). These would be Christian missionaries, like the agitators in Galatia (Galatians 5:12; 6:12-13), who taught that Gentile believers must be circumcised and keep the Law. Whether they were already in Philippi or a danger on the horizon is uncertain: Paul says 'look out', not 'you have been led astray'.

Different groups in 3:2 and 3:18-19. Some think 'the enemies of Christ's cross' whose 'god is the belly' (3:18-19) are a second group, Christians who used freedom as a license for indulgence. Others take both passages as the same people, described with insults.

Non-Christian opponents. A minority reads 3:2 as a warning against local Jews or against pagan cults. Most think this unlikely because Paul answers with arguments about righteousness in Christ. John Chrysostom read the dogs as Jews who 'preached both Christianity and Judaism at the same time' (Homily 10), which is close to the common reading in substance, but his sermon also turned the insult against Jews as a people.

Whatever their identity, Paul's answer is Christ, not a better pedigree: what makes someone belong to God's people is being 'found in him' (3:9).

Paul contrasts two kinds of righteousness: 'a righteousness of my own, the kind that comes from the law', and 'the righteousness that is from God and is based on faith'. Three readings are common.

The Reformation reading. Paul renounces any righteousness earned by keeping the Law and receives a righteousness that God gives and counts to the believer through faith (Augsburg Confession IV: 'This faith God imputes for righteousness in His sight').

The Catholic reading. The righteousness 'from God' is God's gift that truly renews the person. Trent calls it 'the justice of God, not that whereby He Himself is just, but that whereby He maketh us just' (session 6, chapter 7).

The New Perspective. 'My own righteousness' is not merit but the covenant status Paul had as a law-observant Jew, the status his opponents wanted Gentiles to gain by circumcision. Paul gives it up for a righteousness open to all in Christ.

The phrase 'faith in Christ' (literally 'faith of Christ') is itself debated: see the variant entry and the note on 'is based on faith'.

echoes: Genesis 17:10-12; Leviticus 12:3; Deuteronomy 30:6; Jeremiah 4:4; Jeremiah 9:23-24; Numbers 25:11-13; Psalm 8:6; Romans 2:28-29; Romans 3:21-22; Romans 10:2-3; Romans 11:1; 1 Corinthians 9:24-27; 1 Corinthians 15:42-53; 2 Corinthians 11:22; Galatians 1:13-14; Galatians 2:16; Galatians 5:12; Galatians 6:12-14; Acts 9:1-6; Acts 23:6

settings.what: The warning about 'the dogs' and Paul's own story
settings.to: the church at Philippi (see 1:1-2); mostly Gentile believers being warned about opponents whom most readers take to be teachers requiring circumcision
settings.when: after the travel plans; the sudden change of tone at 3:2 may mark the start of a separate letter (debated)
settings.why: on the most common reading, to keep Gentile believers from accepting circumcision and Law-keeping as the price of belonging to God's people. Paul does not argue that Jewish identity is worthless in itself; he shows that he had the best Jewish credentials of anyone and counts them as loss compared with Christ. Knowing that the readers were Gentiles changes the reading: the question is what Gentiles must do to belong, not whether Jews should stop being Jews.
views: Paul turns to a danger he has meant to address, perhaps triggered by news of traveling teachers; 'writing the same things' (3:1) points to earlier warnings.
3:2-4:1 (or 3:2-21) is part of a sharper letter joined to the rest later (Philip Sellew and others).
Jewish-Christian teachers requiring circumcision (the most common view); local Jews; pagan cults; or Christian libertines, perhaps a second group in 3:18-19. See the deep dive.

settings.what: Running for the prize; citizens of heaven
settings.when: as he faces a verdict that may end his race
settings.why: to keep the church from thinking it has arrived, and from following those who live for appetite and earthly things. Paul offers himself as a model, not of perfection but of pursuit. For citizens of a Roman colony, 'we belong to a commonwealth in heaven' tells them where their true status and Lord are, and that their hope is the transformation of their bodies when Christ comes.

traditions.q: Paul wants 'the righteousness that is from God' (3:9), not his own. Is that righteousness counted to the believer, or made the believer's own?
views: The one formal cause of justification is 'the justice of God, not that whereby He Himself is just, but that whereby He maketh us just' (Trent, session 6, chapter 7): God's gift truly renews the person within.

The Confession of Dositheus teaches that a person is 'not simply justified through faith alone, but through faith which works through love', and rejects the idea that faith is only a hand that grasps Christ's righteousness (decree 13).

People 'cannot be justified before God by their own strength, merits, or works' but are freely justified for Christ's sake through faith: 'This faith God imputes for righteousness in His sight' (Augsburg Confession IV).

God justifies 'not by infusing righteousness into them, but by pardoning their sins, and by accounting and accepting their persons as righteous', 'by imputing the obedience and satisfaction of Christ unto them' (Westminster Confession 11.1, which lists Philippians 3:9 among its proof texts).

traditions.q: Paul says he has not 'already been made perfect' (3:12) but calls the mature 'perfect' (3:15). Can a Christian be made perfect in this life?
views: Wesley's sermon 'Christian Perfection' takes 3:12 as its text. Christians are not perfect in knowledge, nor free from mistakes, infirmities or temptation; but 'a Christian is so far perfect, as not to commit sin', and can be 'freed from evil thoughts and evil tempers'.
Sanctification is 'throughout, in the whole man; yet imperfect in this life, there abiding still some remnants of corruption in every part' (Westminster Confession 13.2).

'Believers are not renewed in this life perfectly or completely'; 'the old Adam clings to them right up to the grave', until 'a person is perfectly renewed in the resurrection' (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration VI 7, 18, 24).

All Christians are called 'to the perfection of charity' (Catechism 2013), but in this life it is a road of growth: 'Spiritual progress tends toward ever more intimate union with Christ' (2014), and 'the way of perfection passes by way of the Cross' (2015).

title: Rejoice in the Lord
sum: Paul gathers up the letter. He calls the church his joy and his victory wreath and urges them to stand firm (4:1). He appeals by name to two women, Euodia and Syntyche, who fought at his side for the good news, to think the same way in the Lord, and asks a 'true yokefellow' to help them (4:2-3). Then come short commands: rejoice always, let your gentleness be known, worry about nothing but pray about everything, and God's peace will guard your hearts; think about whatever is true, right and pure (4:4-9).

Last, Paul thanks them for their gift. He has learned to be content in plenty and in want, and he has strength for everything in the one who makes him strong (4:10-13). But they did well to share his trouble, as they did from the beginning, sending help even to Thessalonica; their gift is a sacrifice pleasing to God, and God will meet their every need (4:14-20). Greetings follow, including from 'Caesar's household' (4:21-23).
readings: Read as a thank-you note

Many have noticed that Paul's thanks come at the very end and are carefully worded. In the ancient world a gift could put the receiver under obligation to the giver. Paul's phrasing (he did not need it; God will repay them; the gift is really an offering to God) keeps the relationship one of partnership in the good news, not patronage.
Read as a pastoral letter to a divided church

Others read 4:2-3 as the real point of the letter. The calls to unity in 1:27 and 2:2, and the hymn of humility, prepare for this direct appeal to two leaders in conflict. The commands about joy, gentleness and peace (4:4-7) then apply to the whole church in that situation.

views.H: Women were prominent in the church at Philippi from the start: Lydia hosted it (Acts 16:15, 40), and Euodia and Syntyche were Paul's co-workers. The gift Epaphroditus brought was money or goods carried across the Roman roads; the Via Egnatia ran through Philippi. The 'garrison' picture of 4:7 and 'Caesar's household' (4:22) fit a colony full of Roman soldiers and officials.
views.C: Those who divide Philippians often take 4:10-20 as a separate, earlier thank-you note, sent soon after Epaphroditus arrived; they find it odd that thanks come only at the end of a long letter. Defenders of unity reply that the gift is mentioned at the beginning (1:5) and that ending with it is a deliberate climax. The identity of the 'yokefellow' (4:3) and of Clement are unknown.
views.L: The chapter repeats the letter's key words: stand firm (1:27), think the same (2:2), joy and rejoicing (the thread of the whole letter), partnership (1:5; 4:14-15), and peace. 4:8 uses words common in Greek moral writing and found nowhere else in Paul. The business words of 4:15-18 (account, giving and receiving, paid in full) turn into temple words (a soothing smell, a sacrifice).
views.J: The 'book of life' (4:3) is Israel's image of God's register (Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1). The gift as 'a soothing smell, a sacrifice that God accepts' (4:18) uses the language of Israel's offerings (Genesis 8:21; Numbers 15:10). 'The Lord is near' may echo Psalm 145:18.
views.T: 4:4-6 supplies the opening chant (introit) of the Mass for the third Sunday of Advent in the Western church, 'Gaudete in Domino semper', which gives the day its name, Gaudete Sunday. 4:13 is one of the most quoted verses of the Bible today, often out of context. 4:3 has been cited in debates over women in church leadership; Chrysostom thought Euodia and Syntyche 'seem to me to be the chief of the Church which was there'.

deep.h: Euodia, Syntyche and the women of Philippi
deep.b:
The church at Philippi began with women. Paul's first hearers were 'the women who had gathered' at a place of prayer by a river, and the first convert was Lydia, a dealer in purple cloth who hosted the missionaries and the church (Acts 16:13-15, 40). Some years later two women, Euodia and Syntyche, are important enough that their disagreement is named in a letter read aloud to the whole church.

Paul says they 'fought at my side in spreading the good news', using the athletic word of 1:27, and ranks them with Clement and his other 'fellow workers', the term he uses for Prisca and Aquila, Timothy and Titus (Romans 16:3, 21; 2 Corinthians 8:23). Chrysostom thought they 'seem to me to be the chief of the Church which was there'. Richard Fellows and Alistair Stewart argue that they were householders and patrons of the church.

Paul does not say what they disagreed about. He does not take sides: he appeals to each by name in the same words. He asks a third person, the 'true yokefellow', to help them, which treats the quarrel as a matter for the whole community. How far the passage bears on women's leadership in the church today is debated: see the topic page and the cards at Romans 16:1-7 and 1 Timothy 2.

In the Greek and Roman world a gift was rarely free. A patron gave, a client owed gratitude, loyalty and public praise. Some scholars think the church at Philippi, by supporting Paul, could be heard as becoming his patron, and that Paul's careful thanks avoid this. He rejoices 'in the Lord' (4:10), says he was not in want (4:11), affirms that he can live with little (4:12-13), and describes the gift not as payment to him but as 'fruit' credited to their account (4:17) and as an offering to God (4:18). The one who will repay them is God (4:19).

At the same time Paul is grateful and warm: 'it was kind of you to become partners with me in my hardship' (4:14). Their giving began 'in the early days of the good news' and reached him in Thessalonica twice (4:15-16). The word he uses for it is partnership (koinonia), the word of 1:5. The passage is often used in Christian teaching about giving and about the support of missionaries.

echoes: Exodus 32:32; Psalm 69:28; Daniel 12:1; Psalm 145:18; Genesis 8:21; Numbers 15:10; Matthew 6:25-34; Luke 10:20; Acts 16:13-15; Acts 17:1-9; Romans 16:1-7; 2 Corinthians 8:1-5; 2 Corinthians 11:9; Ephesians 5:2; 1 Thessalonians 2:9; 1 Thessalonians 5:16-18; Revelation 3:5

settings.what: The appeal to Euodia and Syntyche
settings.to: two women co-workers of Paul at Philippi, Euodia and Syntyche, a 'true yokefellow' asked to help them, and the whole church hearing the letter read
settings.when: near the end of the letter, after the calls to unity (1:27; 2:2)
settings.why: to settle a disagreement between two respected co-workers without taking sides, and to involve the church in reconciling them. Naming them in a public letter shows their importance. The appeal uses the letter's key verb, 'think the same way', so the whole letter, the hymn included, becomes the background of this request.

settings.what: Closing commands: joy, gentleness, prayer, peace, and what to think about
settings.when: at the close of the letter's instructions
settings.why: to give a church under pressure and in some conflict a way to live: rejoice in the Lord, be gentle with everyone, turn worry into prayer, and fill the mind with what is good. The promise is the peace of God standing guard like a garrison over their hearts, and the God of peace with them.

settings.to: the church at Philippi (see 1:1-2), who had sent money or goods with Epaphroditus
settings.when: after Epaphroditus' arrival and recovery; some scholars think this section was first sent as a separate, earlier note
settings.why: to thank them warmly without becoming their client or seeming to ask for more. Paul frames the gift as partnership in the good news and as an offering to God, and promises that God will meet their needs. For readers who knew the patron and client customs of the Roman world, this redefines giving among believers.

settings.when: at the end of the letter
settings.why: to send greetings from the believers with Paul, especially those from Caesar's household, which showed the good news reaching people in the emperor's service, and to close with grace as the letter began (1:2).
